nameStory: The round-leaved sundew gets its name from its perfectly circular leaves that sparkle with dewdrops in the morning sun. But here's the twist — those aren't actually dewdrops at all! They're sticky droplets that the plant produces to trap unsuspecting insects, earning it the nickname 'nature's flypaper.'
description: Round-leaved sundew is a tiny carnivorous plant that looks like a miniature alien rosette sitting in wet, mossy areas. The entire plant is only about 1-4 inches across, with perfectly round leaves arranged in a flat circle close to the ground. Each leaf is covered in hundreds of tiny red tentacles that glisten with sticky 'dew' droplets, creating a jewel-like appearance that's both beautiful and deadly to small insects. In summer, it sends up a slender stalk with small white or pink flowers.

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Perfectly round leaves arranged in a flat rosette, each about the size of a dime and covered in hundreds of red, hair-like tentacles that glisten with sticky droplets

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Tiny plant hugging the ground in a flat, circular pattern, typically 1-4 inches across and found nestled among sphagnum moss

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Small white or pale pink flowers on a thin, leafless stalk that rises 2-8 inches above the leaf rosette, blooming from June to August

idTips.label: Texture
idTips.description: Leaves feel incredibly sticky to the touch due to the mucilage droplets — your finger will literally stick to them if you touch the surface

idTips.label: Color Pattern
idTips.description: Bright red tentacles contrast sharply with green leaf centers, creating a distinctive two-toned appearance that's unmistakable

habitat: Found exclusively in acidic, nutrient-poor wetlands including sphagnum bogs, fens, and wet meadows throughout New England. Look for it nestled among cushions of sphagnum moss in areas that stay consistently moist, often alongside bog plants like cranberries, pitcher plants, and cotton grass. It thrives in the acidic conditions where most other plants struggle to survive.

seasonality.spring: New leaf rosettes emerge bright green with developing red tentacles as the weather warms in late April to May.
seasonality.summer: Peak identification time with fully developed sticky leaves and delicate flower stalks blooming from June through August.
seasonality.fall: Leaves may turn more reddish as temperatures drop, but the plant remains active and sticky until frost.
seasonality.winter: Dies back to a small winter bud at ground level, nearly impossible to spot among the dormant sphagnum moss.

funFact: This tiny plant is actually a more efficient predator than many animals — it can digest a trapped insect in just 15 minutes and has been observed catching over 2,000 insects in a single growing season despite being smaller than your palm!
confusionNotes: Most likely confused with its cousin the spoonleaf sundew, but round-leaved sundew has perfectly circular leaves while spoonleaf sundew has oval, spoon-shaped leaves. Memory trick: 'Round' sundew has round leaves — it's right there in the name!
contextualKnowledge: Despite being called 'sundew,' the glistening droplets aren't dew at all but a sticky digestive enzyme called mucilage that the plant produces constantly, even on dry days. Many people are surprised to learn that New England has carnivorous plants at all, but our acidic bogs provide the perfect low-nutrient environment where eating insects gives these plants a survival advantage.
compareHints: Round-leaved sundew differs from spoonleaf sundew by its perfectly circular leaves (versus oval spoon-shaped ones) and typically grows in more open bog areas. Thread-leaved sundew, found rarely in coastal areas, has long thin leaves like green spaghetti rather than the flat round rosette pattern. All three sundew species share the characteristic sticky red tentacles, but the leaf shape is the dead giveaway for identification.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Spoonleaf sundew differs from round-leaved sundew by its spoon-shaped leaves (versus perfectly round) and its tendency to grow in wetter areas.
Unlike its sundew relatives, thread-leaved sundew has long, thin, upright leaves rather than the round, flat leaves of round-leaved sundew or the spoon-shaped leaves of spoonleaf sundew.
